prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B004 for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The chain from human incretin physiology (Holst), proglucagon-derived peptide biology and receptor actions (Drucker) and the identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide (Mojsov) to drugs is original and mechanistically clear. It is confirmed in large independent randomized trials of glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes, and it is mature. The round-1 exchange sharpened my view that the disagreement is about credit and citation wording, not about scientific merit or timing. A discovery-domain citation, which names the physiology and the active form of the peptide, keeps the prize on what the committee can defend as discovery. It also avoids implying that any one drug or company programme is being honoured. I am not relying on the opening count. Every member independently gave a science-based rationale, and I would hold this position if the count were different.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still attribution. Habener's group worked on proglucagon and GLP-1 peptides and is outside the credited names, and Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested. I cannot resolve either point from the supplied record. A physiology-centred trio also leaves out Knudsen, whose long-acting analogues produced the drugs patients take. A reader could say the prize honours the idea but not the delivery. Every three-name set leaves out a defensible contributor. My choice accepts that cost to keep the citation on discovery, and I would say plainly that it is a partial recognition of a larger field.

responses.point: Moved GLP-1 to first place but keeps Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, with a citation that spans physiology and development of incretin-based therapies. He argues that a prize naming only the physiologists omits the person who delivered durable drugs.
responses.response: I take this seriously, and it is the strongest argument against my own trio. Knudsen's work was necessary for the clinical result and is more than industrial routine. Two things keep me with Mojsov. First, the Nobel criterion in this configuration is discovery, and the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is what turned incretin physiology into something that could be targeted. Second, a citation that spans development, as yours does, invites the question of which other developers and trials are omitted, and I do not think the record supports drawing that line. I accept that Mojsov's priority against Habener is unresolved. I would keep her in on the identification and synthesis of the active form, with the citation worded around the peptide and its physiology. If the committee decides it wants drug development in the citation, I would accept Knudsen in place of Mojsov, because that is a coherent and defensible alternative. I will not force consensus on this point.

responses.point: Argues for keeping the citation in the discovery domain, naming the physiology and bioactive forms of GLP-1. She cannot resolve Mojsov's priority against Habener or Knudsen's omission from the supplied material, and she reports no configuration that avoids the cost.
responses.response: I agree that a discovery-domain citation is the cleanest option, and my wording follows hers closely. Our shared uncertainty about Habener should affect the wording and not the names. The citation should say the physiology of GLP-1 and its biologically active form, and should not claim sole credit for first identification of the peptide. That formulation holds whichever way the priority question is later judged. I would not change the laureates because of an unproven priority claim in the absence of evidence in the supplied record. I also share her wish to name the cost openly: the trio is partial and the drug-development contribution is not recognised.

responses.point: Keeps B004 first but warns that a very popular candidate can crowd out one with a cleaner two-person story such as the unfolded protein response (B032, Mori and Walter). He lists B018 and B032 as alternatives and asks whether a two-part prize is worthwhile.
responses.response: The B032 attribution is cleaner than any other on the shortlist, and I accept the crowding concern in principle. My answer is the same as in round 1. A second part would cap the union at three people and reduce the B004 trio to two or one, and B004's own credit problem would then get worse. A B004 plus B032 prize would put the two well-attributed pairs together but would drop Drucker, Holst or Mojsov, and I do not think the B032 case, which is strong on mechanism and weaker on direct medical consequence so far, outweighs that loss. I would keep B032 for a later year. If the committee wants a two-part prize, I would rather give Mori and Walter a part than add a tool or an attribution-gap candidate.

responses.point: Moved from a Drucker, Holst and Knudsen trio to the physiology-centred set after reading attribution arguments. Says that B018 or B043 would be the fallback if credit for B004 proved too tangled, but each has its own attribution gap.
responses.response: I agree with his move and with his fallback logic. B018 and B043 are my alternatives for the same reason, and neither is clean. For B018, Eshhar's original chimeric-receptor concept is outside the supplied names, and the question of whether Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is distinct enough from CAR design is unsettled. For B043, six claimants share three places. I would use either one only if the committee judged B004 too tangled to award. I do not think the B004 credit problem reaches that level, because the physiology chain is well documented and the open question concerns the third name.

uncertainties: Priority for the active GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov versus Habener and other early workers), which I cannot settle from the supplied record.
Whether the committee wants the citation to be limited to discovery or to span drug development; this determines whether Mojsov or Knudsen takes the third place.
For B018 and B043, whether any fair three-person allocation exists given Eshhar and the six-way optogenetics credit.
Whether a second prize part would improve the prize or only reduce the B004 allocation.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I work in autoimmunity and rheumatology, which is adjacent to B018 (CAR-T cells are now used in autoimmune disease), but I have no documented tie to any credited name on the shortlist, and I do not infer relationships from shared institutions or topics. No recusal is needed.
